title: Availability Translation Kit
body:
Objective:
Provide a compact, persona-oriented toolkit that sales, CS, and support can use to translate technical fallback actions into customer-trust language. Include short scripts, expected user-visible effects, and competitor counters.

One-line positioning for decks:
Redwood keeps applications available with explainable fallbacks: measurable, observable routing and quality tradeoffs so customers can make predictable choices during degradation.

Why this matters (buyer insight):
- Buyers don’t just want uptime percentages; they want predictable behavior and clear tradeoffs when things degrade.
- The two core fears: sudden broken flows and opaque recovery. Language that clarifies the action + impact reduces churn.

Primary personas & distilled messages:
- Platform/Infra Engineers: "You can program how traffic moves — region pinning, fallback tiers, and audit logs show exactly when and why a fallback happened."
- Product/ML Engineers: "Fallbacks are quality-aware: we fall back to compact variants with KV prefix caching and reranking to keep core features correct."
- Customer Success / Procurement: "We provide runbooks, contractual SLAs for reserved capacity, and digestible incident timelines."
- Growth/PLG builders: "Default multi-region routing and a read-only cache mode keep you online while you evaluate dedicated options."

Incident archetypes, technical action, and customer scripts:
1) Regional cloud disruption:
- Technical action: automatic routing to healthy region(s), use of compact model variant and cold-cache latency while KV caches rewarm.
- Customer-facing script: "We routed traffic to a nearby healthy region and switched to a compact model variant to maintain throughput. You may see slight latency increases and briefer responses while caches rewarm. We will revert when the primary region is validated healthy."
- Quick CS line: "No data lost — we prioritized availability and will share a timeline and postmortem."

2) Capacity saturation (spike / noisy neighbor / DDoS):
- Technical action: token-limited mode + queuing + priority routing; optional cached-response mode for recurring prompts; enable rate-based shedding for low-priority routes.
- Customer-facing script: "We applied surge controls and prioritized critical requests. Lower-priority calls may be delayed or served from cached prefixes to protect system stability. We can pin critical routes to reserved capacity to avoid this."
- Quick CS line: "We kept your essential flows live by prioritizing them; let’s discuss route pinning for critical paths."

3) Model quality regression or serving bug:
- Technical action: automated rollback to last verified model checkpoint; enable reranker/strict decoding; isolate problematic variant and route away.
- Customer-facing script: "We detected a quality regression and automatically routed to the previously verified model while we investigate. Outputs will be more conservative until we finish the RCA. We’ll share remediation ETA and mitigation details."
- Quick CS proposition: "We rolled back immediately; we’ll deliver a short RCA and recommend a canary policy for your future rollouts."

Tone and trust language guidance:
- Prefer concrete actions over promises. Use "we shifted traffic to X" rather than absolutes like "we prevented".
- Be explicit about tradeoffs: state what was deprioritized (verbosity, latency, freshness) and why.
- Always close with next steps: what we’re doing next, what customers might see, and when they should expect updates.

Channel-specific micro-scripts (short forms):
- In-product banner: "Routing to nearby region to maintain availability. You may see slightly higher latency — update in 15 minutes."
- Support Slack DM: "Automated multi-region failover active for your workspace. We used a compact model to preserve throughput. No action needed; contact us to enable reserved-region capacity."
- Enterprise email subject/body outline: Subject: "Incident update: failover activated — impact & next steps" Body: 1) Summary of action, 2) User-visible impact, 3) Immediate mitigations, 4) ETA for postmortem, 5) Suggested customer actions.

Competitive differentiation (talking points):
- Differentiator: Transparent, programmable fallbacks with audit trails — customers can see the exact timeline and model variant used.
- Practical sell: Offer a demo of Console's fallback timeline and logs during GTM calls to build credibility.
- Counter-obs: Avoid attacking competitors; use evidence-based contrast (e.g., "We surface the fallback timeline and config; many providers don’t expose this by default").

Tactical recommendations for GTM & content:
- Build an "Explain fallback" button in Console that expands to a timeline and applied policy; use this as a trust signal in sales demos.
- Create canned runbooks (region failover, surge, model regression) for SEs to attach to proposals and contracts.
- Run an A/B test for post-incident communications: technical annex vs TL;DR + annex. Measure CS satisfaction and renewal impact.

Incident comms checklist (one-liner):
1) Action taken. 2) User-visible impact. 3) Immediate mitigation + ETA. 4) Link to logs/postmortem timeline. 5) Offer of options (reserved capacity, region pinning).

Appendix: GTM enablement slide suggestions:
- Slide A: Incident archetypes mapped to customer impact (probability x severity).
- Slide B: One-liners per persona for quick roleplay.
- Slide C: Example customer email + in-product banner copy.
- Slide D: Competitive snapshot and handling scripts.

Owner: Sofia Ramirez
Next steps / action items:
- SEs: add a screenshot of the Console fallback timeline to the demo kit.
- Product: evaluate one-click "explain fallback" prototype by end of quarter.
- CS: prepare two post-incident email templates (tech-heavy and exec-friendly).

Relevant artifacts and refs: /display/OPS/Multi-region+Failover+Runbook, RUN-1283, https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/3124

End of document.
